idiom_name: immutable snapshot + guarded rebind (dict.copy, MappingProxyType, frozen dataclasses); pandas Copy-on-Write as the library-grade form
implementation_notes: CPython already reference-counts every object (atomically, under the GIL; biased and per-thread counting in free-threaded builds), so user code never writes the counted body - it writes the publish step: hold the shared state in one name and replace it with a fresh snapshot under a threading.Lock. Readers take the snapshot once and use it without a lock; dict.copy() builds the shallow snapshot (copy.deepcopy for nested state), MappingProxyType publishes a read-only view, and frozen dataclasses or tuples make the snapshot's own structure immutable. In data workloads the pattern arrives as a guarantee of the library instead: pandas made Copy-on-Write the default in 3.0, so 'any DataFrame or Series derived from another in any way always behaves as a copy' and most methods avoid copying until a write forces it. A hand-written count stays justified only when wrapping buffers whose lifetime lives outside the interpreter (mmap or a C-extension buffer).
code_sketch:
import threading
from types import MappingProxyType

_lock = threading.Lock()
_routes = MappingProxyType({})            # published snapshot

def lookup(k):                            # readers: no lock, coherent snapshot
    return _routes.get(k)
def add(k, v):
    global _routes
    with _lock:                           # writers serialise
        nxt = dict(_routes)               # copy-on-write
        nxt[k] = v
        _routes = MappingProxyType(nxt)   # publish
pitfalls: Snapshots are shallow and copying is O(n) per write: nested containers stay shared, so mutating a nested dict mutates every snapshot that referenced it - deep-freeze or rebuild the whole path, and batch updates into one copy per transaction.

The GIL is not a synchronisation plan: check-then-act on the snapshot (read, compute, publish) races with another writer unless the whole sequence holds the lock, and the free-threading documentation recommends threading.Lock rather than relying on the internal locks of built-in types.

Rebinding is not updating: code that captured a local reference to the old snapshot keeps reading the old one (which is exactly the snapshot guarantee), but code that stores the snapshot in a mutable container and mutates that container has silently broken publication.
sources: pandas documentation, Copy-on-Write (CoW) - CoW is the default in pandas 3.0; 'any DataFrame or Series derived from another in any way always behaves as a copy' and most methods 'only trigger a copy when necessary': https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/copy_on_write.html

Python documentation, Python support for free threading - built-in types use internal locks, and 'It's recommended to use the threading.Lock or other synchronization primitives instead of relying on the internal locks of built-in types': https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html
